title: How to quote pickup times on restaurant calls
seoTitle: How to quote pickup time for restaurants
description: Quote pickup times clearly on restaurant calls, handle rush periods, and keep orders accurate without overpromising.
question: How do I quote pickup time on restaurant phone orders without overpromising?
answer: Quote pickup times from your real kitchen pace, not a guess. Say the time in a simple, specific way, and add a small buffer for rush periods, large orders, or items that take longer. Keep one standard script for staff and use the same rule every time so callers hear the same kind of answer.
summary: You’ll learn a simple way to quote pickup times that matches kitchen reality and sounds clear on the phone.
intro:
Quoting pickup time on the phone should be simple: tell the caller the time you can actually have the order ready, and do not promise sooner than the kitchen can cook it. A clear pickup time helps the caller decide, and it helps your team avoid rushed mistakes.

For many restaurants, the hard part is not taking the order. It is giving a time that fits the line, the oven, the fryers, and the people in the store. ROAL handles that by taking the order from the live menu, confirming it, and quoting a ready time on the call, while tricky calls still go to staff.

sections.h2: How should I quote a pickup time on the phone?
sections.body:
Use a short, confident time quote that matches your real prep pace. Do not say “maybe 15 minutes” unless you really mean it. Say the time in a way the caller can repeat back.

A simple script works best:
- “For that pickup order, we can have it ready in about 20 minutes.”
- “Right now we’re running about 35 minutes for pickup.”
- “That item takes a little longer, so I’m quoting 40 minutes.”

If your kitchen has a steady rhythm, use a standard starting point for common orders. For example, you might tell callers that a sandwich order is about 15 to 20 minutes, while a pizza order is closer to 25 to 30 minutes. Use your own real numbers. The goal is to be clear enough that the caller knows when to leave, but flexible enough that your staff is not boxed in by a promise you cannot keep.

A good rule is: quote the time you expect now, not the best-case time. If the line is already busy, add a small buffer before you speak.

sections.h2: What should I say when the kitchen is busy?
sections.body:
Busy calls need a calm, honest answer. The caller usually cares more about a real ready time than a perfect one. If you are slammed, say so in plain language and give the next workable pickup window.

Example script:
- “We’re a little backed up right now. The earliest pickup time I can give you is 45 minutes.”
- “We can take that order, and the soonest pickup is about 30 minutes.”
- “Because we’re in a rush, I don’t want to underquote it. I’m putting you at 50 minutes.”

Here is a simple way to decide the quote:
1. Look at the current ticket line.
2. Add your normal cook time for that item.
3. Add extra time for large orders or special requests.
4. Tell the caller the earliest time that still feels safe.

If you use ROAL, it can quote a ready time while taking the order and send the ticket to the kitchen screen. That matters because the host can keep the wording steady while your team focuses on the line. For more on that flow, see [pickup order taking](/use-cases/pickup-orders) and [phone order script templates](/blog/phone-order-script-restaurant).

sections.h2: How do I handle large orders and add-ons without delaying everyone?
sections.body:
Large pickup orders usually need a different time than a single lunch combo. A caller ordering six entrees, extra sauces, and a couple of modifiers is asking for more kitchen time, even if they do not realize it. Quote the time based on the whole order, not just the first item.

Use a worked example like this, then plug in your own numbers:
- Say your standard small order is ready in 20 minutes.
- Say an extra 5 minutes is needed for every few additional items.
- Say a large order with multiple sides and modifiers pushes you to 35 minutes.

A practical script:
- “That’s a bigger order, so I’m quoting 35 minutes for pickup.”
- “With the extra sides and modifications, I want to give you a safe ready time of 40 minutes.”

Short checklist before you confirm the time:
- Count the number of items.
- Check for modifiers, well-done requests, or extra toppings.
- Think about whether any item takes longer than the rest.
- Add a buffer if the order is for the dinner rush.

If you want a deeper checklist for messy orders, see [the most common phone order mistakes](/blog/phone-order-mistakes-restaurants) and [taking large phone orders without errors](/blog/large-phone-orders-restaurant).

sections.h2: How do I quote pickup time for different menu items?
sections.body:
Not every menu item moves at the same speed. Fries, fried apps, and cooked-to-order dishes usually need more honest timing than cold items. If you quote the same time for everything, you end up underestimating the slow items and overpromising the fast ones.

A simple table can help staff stay consistent:

| Order type | Example quote | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| Cold sandwich or deli item | 10-15 minutes | Short prep, but still check the line |
| Hot sandwich or fried item | 15-20 minutes | Add time when the fryer is busy |
| Pizza or baked item | 20-30 minutes | Depends on oven load |
| Large mixed order | 30-45 minutes | Add time for modifiers and sides |

Use these only as starting examples. Replace them with the times your kitchen can actually hit. If an item is sold out, do not offer it. If a caller asks for something that takes longer than normal, say so directly: “That item will add a few extra minutes, so I’m quoting 30 minutes instead of 20.”

ROAL reads the live menu and does not offer sold-out items, which helps reduce those awkward phone corrections. But even with any phone host, the real rule stays the same: quote the ready time based on the order in front of you, not on hope.

sections.h2: What exact phone script sounds clear to customers?
sections.body:
A clean pickup-time script should be short, polite, and easy to repeat. Do not ramble. Say the time, then confirm the pickup name and phone number, and then read the order back.

Here is a practical script you can train staff on:
- “Thanks. We can have that ready in about 25 minutes.”
- “Pickup name, please?”
- “And the best phone number in case we need to reach you?”
- “Let me read that back to make sure I have it right.”

If the caller pushes for sooner, keep the answer firm but friendly:
- “I don’t want to promise too early. 25 minutes is the safest time I can give you.”
- “If anything changes, I’ll tell you now, but 25 minutes is what we can do.”

A simple confirmation checklist:
- Pickup time quoted clearly.
- Name collected.
- Phone number collected.
- Order read back.
- Any special notes repeated.

This matters because a pickup quote is part of the order promise. If you want more help with the read-back step, see [why you should read back every phone order](/blog/read-back-phone-orders). That habit helps catch wrong sizes, wrong toppings, and wrong times before the caller hangs up.

sections.h2: How do I set the timing rule for my own restaurant?
sections.body:
The best pickup-time rule is the one your kitchen can actually keep on a normal day. Start with a simple baseline and adjust it after a few busy shifts. Write the rule down so everyone says the same thing.

Here is a starter process you can use:
1. Pick a baseline time for your most common order.
2. Add a second time for busy periods.
3. Add a third time for large orders or items that take longer.
4. Tell the person answering the phone exactly when to use each one.

Example:
- Slow period: “about 15 minutes.”
- Normal period: “about 20 minutes.”
- Rush period: “about 30 to 40 minutes.”

You can also build this into your phone habits. If you forward calls when busy, confirm with your carrier or phone system first. Codes vary by carrier and plan, and you should always test with a call. For a quick reference, see [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes).

If you want a phone host that can keep that timing rule steady across calls, ROAL is set up to do that while your team stays focused on the kitchen. For owners who want to try it, the easiest next step is to [build a free test host from your website](/try).

takeaways: Quote pickup time from the kitchen’s real pace, not from a guess.
Use one clear script so every caller hears the same timing style.
Add a buffer for rush periods, large orders, and longer-cook items.
Confirm the time, then confirm the name, phone number, and order details.

faq.q: What is the best way to quote pickup time on the phone?
faq.a: Give a specific ready time based on the current kitchen line and the items ordered. Keep the wording short, like “about 20 minutes,” and avoid promising a time you cannot keep. If the restaurant is busy, add a small buffer and say that plainly.

faq.q: How do I handle pickup time during a dinner rush?
faq.a: Use the earliest time your kitchen can safely hit, then say it clearly. For example: “We’re running about 45 minutes for pickup right now.” That kind of quote is better than underestimating and making the caller wait in the lobby.

faq.q: Should I give the same pickup time for every order?
faq.a: No. Small orders, large orders, and items that take longer should not all get the same quote. Use a baseline, then add time for modifiers, multiple items, and rush periods so the quote matches the work.
